title: DevOps & CI/CD
description: Containerise applications with Docker, automate deployments with GitHub Actions, and ship code confidently with blue-green and canary strategies.

topics.title: Docker: Containers from Scratch
topics.content:
### Why Containers?

Before Docker, the classic problem was "it works on my machine". A container packages your app **and its entire runtime** — Node version, OS libraries, config — into one portable unit. Run it anywhere a Docker daemon exists and it behaves identically.

A container is not a VM. It shares the host OS kernel but has its own filesystem, networking, and process space. This makes containers start in milliseconds and use far less RAM than VMs.

#### Your First Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Start from an official base image
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency manifests first (layer caching trick)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# The command to run when the container starts
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

#### Why Copy package.json First?

Docker caches each layer. If you copy all source files first, every code change invalidates the `npm install` layer, making builds slow. By copying `package*.json` separately, the install layer is only re-run when dependencies change.

```
Layer 1: FROM node:20-alpine          ← cached forever
Layer 2: COPY package*.json ./        ← only changes when deps change
Layer 3: RUN npm ci                   ← only re-runs when layer 2 changes
Layer 4: COPY . .                     ← invalidated on every code change
Layer 5: CMD ["node", "src/index.js"] ← cheap metadata
```

#### Multi-Stage Builds

For compiled languages (TypeScript, Go) or apps with heavy dev dependencies, use multi-stage builds to produce a tiny production image:

```dockerfile
# --- Stage 1: Build ---
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci                    # includes devDependencies
COPY . .
RUN npm run build             # compiles TypeScript → dist/

# --- Stage 2: Production ---
FROM node:20-alpine AS production
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production  # only production deps
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist   # copy compiled output
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
```

The final image contains no TypeScript compiler, no source maps, no test dependencies — just what's needed to run.

#### .dockerignore

Like `.gitignore`, this prevents files from being sent to the Docker build context:

```
node_modules
.git
*.log
dist
.env
.env.*
README.md
```

Without this, `node_modules` (hundreds of MB) would be copied on every build.

#### Essential Docker Commands

```bash
# Build an image, tag it
docker build -t myapp:latest .

# Run a container
docker run -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env myapp:latest

# Run in background (detached)
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --name myapp myapp:latest

# View running containers
docker ps

# Stream logs
docker logs -f myapp

# Open a shell inside a running container
docker exec -it myapp sh

# Stop and remove
docker stop myapp && docker rm myapp

# Remove all stopped containers + dangling images
docker system prune
```

topics.title: Docker Compose: Multi-Container Apps
topics.content:
### Running Your Full Stack Locally

A real app needs multiple services: the API server, a database, a cache, maybe a message queue. Docker Compose lets you define all of them in one `docker-compose.yml` file and start everything with one command.

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
version: '3.9'

services:
  api:
    build: .                        # build from local Dockerfile
    ports:
      - '3000:3000'
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=development
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/mydb
      - REDIS_URL=redis://cache:6379
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_started
    volumes:
      - ./src:/app/src               # hot-reload: mount source code

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
      POSTGRES_DB: mydb
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data   # persist data
    healthcheck:
      test: ['CMD-SHELL', 'pg_isready -U user']
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: redis-server --maxmemory 256mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

volumes:
  postgres_data:
```

#### Service Discovery

Inside Docker Compose, services talk to each other by **service name**. The API connects to `db:5432` — Docker's internal DNS resolves `db` to the postgres container's IP. You never hardcode IP addresses.

#### Key Compose Commands

```bash
# Start all services (build if needed)
docker compose up --build

# Start in background
docker compose up -d

# View logs from all services
docker compose logs -f

# View logs from one service
docker compose logs -f api

# Run a command in a service
docker compose exec db psql -U user -d mydb

# Stop everything
docker compose down

# Stop and delete volumes (wipe database)
docker compose down -v

# Rebuild a single service
docker compose up --build api
```

#### Separating Dev and Prod Configs

```yaml
# docker-compose.override.yml (auto-loaded in dev)
services:
  api:
    command: npm run dev           # use nodemon/tsx in dev
    volumes:
      - ./src:/app/src             # live reload
    environment:
      - DEBUG=true
```

In production, use the base `docker-compose.yml` only — no volume mounts, no dev servers.

topics.title: GitHub Actions: CI/CD Pipelines
topics.content:
### Automating Quality Gates and Deployment

Every time you push code, GitHub Actions can automatically run tests, check types, build Docker images, and deploy — giving you instant feedback and preventing broken code from reaching production.

#### A Complete CI Pipeline

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
          POSTGRES_DB: testdb
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5
        ports:
          - 5432:5432

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Type check
        run: npm run type-check

      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:testpass@localhost:5432/testdb
          JWT_SECRET: test-secret-for-ci

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build
```

#### CD Pipeline: Build and Push Docker Image

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: test           # only deploy if tests pass
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          push: true
          tags: |
            myorg/myapp:latest
            myorg/myapp:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: build-and-push
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to server
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_HOST }}
          username: deploy
          key: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY }}
          script: |
            docker pull myorg/myapp:latest
            docker compose -f /app/docker-compose.prod.yml up -d --no-deps api
```

#### Managing Secrets

Secrets are stored in GitHub: `Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions`. In workflows they're accessed as `${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }}`. They are:
- Never printed in logs
- Not passed to forked repo PRs (security)
- Available as environment variables at runtime

#### Branch Protection Rules

In GitHub `Settings → Branches`, require:
- Status checks must pass before merging (your CI job)
- Require PR reviews before merging
- Dismiss stale reviews when new commits are pushed

This makes `main` a deploy-grade branch at all times.

topics.title: Deployment Strategies
topics.content:
### Shipping Without Downtime

How you deploy matters as much as what you deploy. Dropping your app during an update is unacceptable. Here are the main strategies, from simplest to most sophisticated.

#### Rolling Deployment

The default for most orchestrated systems. New instances are brought up gradually, old ones are terminated as new ones pass health checks.

```
v1  v1  v1  v1    →    v2  v1  v1  v1    →    v2  v2  v1  v1    →    v2  v2  v2  v2
```

- No extra infrastructure needed
- Requires your app to be backwards-compatible during the transition (both v1 and v2 run simultaneously)
- If v2 fails health checks, the rollout pauses or rolls back automatically

#### Blue-Green Deployment

Two identical production environments. "Blue" is live. Deploy to "green", test it, then flip the load balancer.

```
                  Load Balancer
                       │
          ┌────────────┴────────────┐
     ┌────▼────┐               ┌───▼─────┐
     │  BLUE   │               │  GREEN  │
     │  (live) │               │ (new v) │
     └─────────┘               └─────────┘

  1. Deploy new version to GREEN
  2. Run smoke tests against GREEN
  3. Switch load balancer to GREEN
  4. BLUE becomes standby (instant rollback)
```

- **Instant rollback**: flip the load balancer back
- Requires 2x infrastructure cost
- Database migrations must be backwards-compatible

#### Canary Deployment

Route a small percentage of real traffic to the new version. Gradually increase if metrics look good.

```nginx
# nginx upstream with canary weight
upstream app {
  server stable:3000  weight=90;   # 90% of traffic
  server canary:3000  weight=10;   # 10% of traffic (canary)
}
```

Monitor error rates, latency, and business metrics for the canary. If they're healthy, increase the weight. If they degrade, route 0% to canary and investigate.

#### Database Migrations: The Hard Part

The trickiest part of zero-downtime deployment is schema changes. The golden rule:

**Never deploy a migration and application change simultaneously.** Always separate them into two deploys.

```
# WRONG: Deploy migration + code change together
# While v2 code runs, old v1 servers still read/write old schema → CRASH

# RIGHT: Expand-then-contract pattern

Deploy 1: Add new column (nullable)   ← v1 code still works
Deploy 2: Deploy new code using column ← both v1 and v2 work
Deploy 3: Remove old column           ← after v1 is fully gone
```

#### Graceful Shutdown

When a server is terminated, it should finish in-flight requests before exiting:

```js
const server = app.listen(3000);

// Handle SIGTERM (sent by Docker/K8s to stop the container)
process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
  console.log('SIGTERM received. Shutting down gracefully...');

  // Stop accepting new connections
  server.close(async () => {
    // Wait for in-flight requests to complete
    await db.pool.end();   // close DB connection pool
    await redis.quit();    // close Redis connections
    console.log('Server shut down.');
    process.exit(0);
  });

  // Force shutdown if graceful shutdown takes too long
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.error('Forced shutdown after timeout');
    process.exit(1);
  }, 30_000);
});
```
